$30. For almost 10,000 miles.

That's what one EV owner spent on charging, total, because his job has a free plug in the parking lot. He drives 100 miles round trip every day. On gas he was spending over $400 a month. And half of that $30 was him trying out Superchargers for fun.

Most of us aren't that lucky. Average home charging runs about $6.75 per 100 miles. Fast chargers on the road are closer to $18.55.

drafts.title: $2,800 for labor on a 'free' warranty battery swap
drafts.angle: One question to ask before you sign for a home battery: who pays labor if it fails and your installer is gone? Soft battery slot; useful and save-worthy.
bullets: Seattle-area Powerwall 3 failed after about a year; Tesla approved a warranty module swap.
The original installer had gone out of business.
Other installers quoted $2,000 to $2,800 in labor, or refused the job.
Parts warranties often exclude labor unless it is a recall.
drafts.body: $2,800 for labor on a 'free' warranty battery swap. His installer went out of business. Before I buy a battery, I'm asking {who pays labor if it fails}. Did your installer put that in writing?
drafts.framework_body:
$2,800. That's the labor bill on a battery swap that was supposed to be free.

A homeowner near Seattle had his Powerwall fail after about a year. Tesla said fine, warranty, we'll send the part. Good so far.

Then the problem. The company that installed it had gone out of business. Other installers wanted $2,000 to $2,800 just to do the swap, and some wouldn't touch it.

The warranty covered the battery. Nobody covered the guy holding the wrench.

I'm still on the fence about a home battery. {where I am on it}. But this goes on my list of questions before I sign anything: who pays labor if it fails, and what happens if you're gone in five years?

Did your installer put that in writing?
drafts.ocr_why: Practical and save-worthy, but batteries are a soft-pedal lane, so it sits in the fifth slot.
